MAHA Adviser, Unhappy at Pace, Quits Administration
|                                                       By                             Bob Cronin                                 withNewser.AI                                                                                   Posted Oct 22, 2026  4:50 PM CDT                                                       | 
A key architect of Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s "Make America Healthy Again" campaign is leaving the Trump administration, frustrated at the pace of change. Calley Means, a senior adviser to Kennedy who had been working out of the White House on food and nutrition policy, resigned Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reports. People familiar with the situation said Means grew exasperated as the White House stalled on several Kennedy-backed food initiatives, including an official definition of "ultraprocessed" foods and new rules to cut added sugar and boost protein in school meals.
Others in the MAHA movement share Means' frustration, Politico reports. It's had successes with the administration's backing has but been disappointed by administration actions aiding the pesticide industry, as well as promises to change food policy that haven't been carried out. Means, who reportedly clashed with colleagues in the West Wing, issued a statement saying he still supports Trump and Kennedy. "This movement is in the first inning and just getting started," he said.

sources.news_title: Calley Means, a key MAHA advocate, resigns as a top RFK Jr. adviser – WTOP News
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday.
In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration’s lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate.
Means said he “leaves with tremendous respect” for President Donald Trump and Kennedy.
“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick,” Means said. “This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”
Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation’s leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests.
White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is “grateful” for Means’ time and “he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement.” A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment.
Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is “impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests.”
“At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation’s health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself,” she said.
Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance.
Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans.
Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry.
At the same time, Means’ emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on “medical freedom” issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines.
Despite Means’ efforts, the administration’s progress on food reforms has been slow going.
Kennedy had promised the release of a first-ever government definition of ultraprocessed food in April. Instead, FDA’s acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, told a conference that month that defining the class “is really hard.”
In August, Kennedy staffers again suggested an announcement on the issue was imminent. Instead, the announcement focused on a proposal bringing greater scrutiny to food additives. It made only passing mention of ultraprocessed foods.

sources.news_title: Top RFK Jr. Adviser Calley Means Resigns Amid Reported Frustration Over Delayed Health Reforms
Top RFK Jr. adviser Calley Means resigns from Trump administration
Top RFK Jr. Adviser Resigns
sources.text:
A top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is stepping down.
Calley Means, who has worked on a range of Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiatives, did not disclose a reason for his resignation on Oct. 22, and said he has tremendous respect for both Kennedy and President Donald Trump.
“They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick. More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started,” Means wrote on X.
“It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from [food stamps], removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.”
The White House and the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.
Means, 41, founded a company called Truemed in 2022, which focused on letting people spend money from health savings accounts and similar tranches on health products, and later co-authored a book with his sister, Dr. Casey Means.
Means has frequently spoken at press briefings and on social media about steps the Trump administration has taken to clean up food, including banning several synthetic dyes and pressuring companies to voluntarily remove others, and updating the food pyramid.
“History will remember the first two years of the Trump administration as the most significant food reform in modern history,” Means said at a briefing earlier this year.
Dr. Casey Means was selected by Trump with Kennedy’s backing to be surgeon general, another post in the Department of Health and Human Services, but withdrew after facing opposition in the Senate.

sources.news_title: MAHA Leader Calley Means Steps Down from Trump Administration Health Advisory Role
sources.text:
Calley Means, one of the key figures in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, said on Thursday that he was stepping down from his role as a senior health adviser in the Trump Administration.
In a post on X, Means said that he was resigning “with tremendous respect” for President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick,” Means said. “More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started.”
News outlets including the New York Times and POLITICO, citing anonymous sources with knowledge of the situation, have reported that Means was becoming increasingly frustrated because he felt that there was little movement on issues central to the MAHA agenda—for instance, on the issue of defining and regulating ultraprocessed foods.
Means, who was pivotal in coordinating an alliance between Kennedy and Trump during the 2024 election cycle, has championed the Administration's food-policy agenda, including efforts to persuade manufacturers to stop using artificial food dyes in their products and to restrict the purchase of soda with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits in some states.
In his social media post, Means heralded those actions, as well as his efforts to reform dietary guidelines and his push for research into psychedelic medications.
“It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration,” Means said.
Means is the latest figure in the Trump Administration, and specifically in the Department of Health and Human Services, to resign or be ousted from their role over the past year. In May, Dr. Marty Makary stepped down as the head of the Food and Drug Administration amid pressure from within and outside of the Trump Administration. Last year, the White House fired Susan Monarez as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In April, Trump withdrew his nomination of MAHA leader Dr. Casey Means—Calley Means’ sister—for the position of U.S. Surgeon General after the nomination failed to garner enough support in the Senate.

sources.news_title: Key Architect Of Make America Health Again Alliance Resigns
sources.text:
A chief architect of the alliance between President Donald Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. resigned from the White House on Thursday, citing frustration with what he described as “dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick.”
Calley Means, an author, wellness entrepreneur, and advocate for reforms to nutrition policy, arranged a phone call during the 2024 election that helped clinch Kennedy’s endorsement of Trump campaign. Trump would later appoint Kennedy as secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, the nation’s most powerful official overseeing health policy.
“I don’t know him very well,” Trump said in a gaggle with reporters Thursday afternoon, before adding “MAHA is great.”
For months, administration officials have stressed that food policy would be central for motivating the Kennedy supporters who backed Trump two years ago to pull the lever for Republicans in the midterm elections. Just 12 days before Election Day, Means, a key driver of the administration’s food policy, has publicly indicated the administration is obstructing those changes.
I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy. They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick. More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history - and I know this movement is just getting started. It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.
— Calley Means (@calleymeans) October 22, 2026
Means nevertheless expressed optimism that the MAHA movement will continue to be a political force, and named as key achievements the new dietary guidelines, expanded access to psychedelics to treat mental health, deals with major food companies to remove food dyes and reforms to chemicals allowed in food as “generally recognized as safe.”
“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history — and I know this movement is just getting started,” he said.
The White House canceled a meeting Thursday with Means and Kennedy on clarifying a federal definition of “ultra-processed foods,” Politico reported. Someone familiar with the plans had leaked the meeting to POLITICO last week, framing it as an action that could help shore up disaffected MAHA voters.
Two proposed rules on food changes are currently under consideration at the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), a regulation that would replace the antiquated “generally recognized as safe” (GRAS) pathway that allowed food companies to introduce new additives without notifying the FDA. A second regulation would standardize the federal definition of “ultra-processed foods,” a tweak that could affect school lunches, food labels and dietary guidelines.
Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
Means had grated on some administration officials with his aggressive pushes for reform amid bureaucratic processes that are by nature slow, according to current and former administration officials who were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters.
But one former official said bureaucratic obstacles are sometimes used as an excuse to hold up policies unpopular with influential corporations.
“He was the last principled warrior willing to stand up to corruption and special interests,” another former official said.
In February, President Donald Trump signed an executive order invoking the Defense Production Act to prioritize the domestic supply of glyphosate, trademarked as Roundup, which some scientific evidence links to cancer, liver and kidney disease, endocrine disruption and neurotoxicity.
By May, Food and Drug Administration Commissioner Marty Makary had resigned under pressure, and a top aide on pharmaceutical policy was fired following a string of headlines about drugmakers’ anger with their changes.
Administration officials stressed a pivot away from headline noise about vaccines and the pharmaceutical industry and toward nutrition policy before the midterm elections, citing polling by Trump’s go-to pollster Tony Fabrizio.
In fact, Fabrizio found in a separate poll that was never released in full that a bipartisan majority of voters do not trust the pharmaceutical industry (90%) and express concerns about vaccine mandates (73%), the Daily Caller News Foundation first reported.
Reports of a pivot to nutrition policy to the exclusion of pharmaceutical policy rattled critics of the mRNA platform that undergirds Pfizer’s and Moderna’s COVID vaccines. They wrote in an open letter of a “bait and switch” that “rebranded the grassroots powerful objection to the damaging mRNA platform as a concern about coloring agents in Skittles.”
Now Means, the most visible advocate for changes to the dyes in food products like Skittles, has also resigned.

sources.text:
Trump’s top MAHA ally just resigned over stalled agenda
‘I know this movement is just getting started,’ Calley Means wrote in his resignation post

Calley Means, a senior adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a leading figure in the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned Thursday.
He had reportedly grown frustrated with what he viewed as a stalled agenda and had come to believe that special interests were undermining the movement, according to Politico.
“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote on X. “They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick.”
“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history - and I know this movement is just getting started,” he added.
Means, a Stanford graduate and co-founder of the wellness company Truemed, worked on Kennedy’s failed 2024 presidential campaign, before becoming a senior HHS adviser last year.
During his tenure, he helped advance several administration initiatives, including revisions to federal nutrition guidelines, efforts to phase out synthetic food dyes and expanded research into psychedelic treatments for mental illness.
His exit from the administration — less than two weeks before the midterm elections — followed growing disillusionment with what he saw as a failure to meaningfully advance MAHA priorities, Politico reported, citing two U.S. officials.
Means was scheduled to meet with White House officials and Kennedy this week to talk about policies for ultraprocessed foods — but the sit-down was pushed back.
“That was the straw that broke the camel’s back,” one unnamed official told the outlet. “Calley’s been pushing very, very hard for this, but it’s been a very opaque process and has been just continuously stonewalled.”
Other supporters of MAHA — a loose coalition of Kennedy allies focused on wellness and combating chronic disease — saw the president’s February executive order boosting production of glyphosate, an herbicide, as a sign the movement was losing ground.
“There are a lot of presidential promises within the MAHA movement that have been pretty blatantly subverted by special interests, and that’s completely driving his decision to step to step aside and resign,” an unnamed official said.
In May, CNN reported that Kennedy’s allies expressed concern that the secretary was being “marginalized” by the Trump administration, a claim that the White House denied.
“Making America Healthy Again has been a Day One priority for President Trump, and Secretary Kennedy continues to play a central role in the Trump administration’s whole-of-government effort to deliver on the President’s MAHA agenda,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai said at the time.
A March Politico survey revealed that nearly half of MAHA voters do not think Trump has done enough to champion their causes. An April poll found that 14 percent of voters identified as being part of the MAHA movement.

sources.news_title: MAHA White House adviser Calley Means resigns
Key Trump health adviser resigns before midterm elections - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
WASHINGTON -- Calley Means, a leader of the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from the Trump administration Thursday, signaling a further erosion of a coalition that helped propel President Donald Trump to power a second time.
Means, a top adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services, was a key official behind policies around food quality, including an effort to increase disclosure of the chemicals in food, remove artificial food dyes and ban soda from the federal food assistance program known as SNAP.
He also worked on an executive order to support the development of psychedelic medications.
“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and R.F.K. Jr. -- two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt D.C. bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement, referring to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
In recent months, though, he began to feel stymied in his attempts to deliver on promises to improve the food supply, such as by defining ultraprocessed foods, an initial step to regulating them, according to a person close to him.
Vani Hari, a MAHA leader and healthy eating influencer, said that a turning point for Means came when the White House roiled the MAHA movement with an executive order supporting the increased production of glyphosate, a pesticide that the movement is particularly focused on eliminating.
The second Trump administration secured agreements from food companies that pledged to remove artificial dyes and seed oils from their products. Means also played a key role in MAHA reports outlining goals to reduce chronic disease in children.
Means could be outspoken and direct and was a pugnacious profile on social media. In recent days, his frustration became apparent in his posts on one of his signature issues -- the health effects of ultraprocessed food consumption, which he said was “highly tied to our chronic disease crisis that is killing Americans and bankrupting our country.”
Still, he wrote in his resignation statement that “the past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and health care incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”
Trump last year nominated Means’ sister, Casey Means, to be surgeon general but withdrew her when it became clear that she did not have enough Senate votes for confirmation.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

(CNN) — Calley Means, a prominent figure in the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, resigned from his position as a senior Trump health official on Thursday over frustrations with the government’s progress tackling chronic disease, according to multiple people familiar with his decision.
Means confirmed his departure in a statement, that he is resigning “with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy.”
A top adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Means’ exit comes mounting frustration from MAHA supporters over government inaction on ultraprocessed foods and pesticides.
It represents the latest blow to the political alliance between the president’s “Make America Great Again” base and Kennedy’s MAHA voters, who helped power Trump to the White House in 2024, only for them to grow increasingly disillusioned as their key food and health priorities stalled.
This month, a coalition of MAHA activists released a “scorecard” claiming the administration had failed most of its promises to restrict pesticide use, promote healthier foods and break up special interests in Washington.
Means, who was widely credited with introducing Kennedy to Trump – eventually leading the former to endorse him and end up in his Cabinet – had served as one of Kennedy’s closest outside advisers before officially joining the administration. He held a temporary role at the White House, then later became a top adviser at HHS. Trump nominated his sister, Casey Means, as surgeon general, though this was later withdrawn.
MAHA unhappy with delays
Means, who had championed Trump as a candidate willing to overhaul the government’s approach to food and health regulation, grew increasingly frustrated over delays in advancing a series of policies at the center of the MAHA agenda, three people familiar with the matter said.
Trump health officials had initially hoped that policies, including an effort to create a definition for ultraprocessed foods, would be finalized well before the midterm elections. Instead, they’ve faced continued delays in the White House and sharp pushback from major agriculture industry groups.
Means decided to quit primarily because of those delays, the people familiar with his thinking said.
He is the latest in a string of senior health officials who have quit or been fired in recent months as voters soured on Kennedy’s controversial vaccine policies and the White House sought to pivot its health agenda toward more popular policy priorities.
In August, Means stood alongside Kennedy at an HHS event where the secretary promised a slew of policies aimed at cracking down on artificial food dyes, sweeteners and other additives in popular foods.
But their announcement stopped short of requiring food manufacturers to prove their ingredients are safe – a long-held priority for MAHA advocates.
The delay has stoked anger among MAHA advocates promising retribution at the ballot box.
Means, in a post on X, said that Kennedy and Trump “laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick” and have made significant progress in the past two years. “More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history - and I know this movement is just getting started,” he wrote.
Allison Schuster, a spokesperson for the White House, said: “We are grateful for Calley Means’ time in the Trump Administration. He has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement.”
Kelly Ryerson, a MAHA advocate known for her activism on pesticides, said of Means: “I am impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests.”
“Sophisticated legal roadblocks and political shenanigans designed to appease corporate interests have made progress nearly impossible,” Ryerson added. “Big Food and Big Ag only continue to survive by owning our elected officials and regulators, and they are currently succeeding.”
“It’s devastating, but had to be done,” Alex Clark, an influencer who runs a popular MAHA-themed podcast for Turning Point USA, said, referring to Means’ exit. “I would have had no choice but to leave too.”
This story has been updated with additional information.

Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a co-author of the so-called “MAHA bible”—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement.
“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote in a social media post this afternoon. “It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.”
His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy.
Sources close to Means told The Wall Street Journal that he had grown frustrated in the position. One source described Means as “disillusioned.”

In recent meetings, Means reportedly raised his voice and grew visibly frustrated over the lack of progress on such issues. Others in the administration complained he was unwilling to make political concessions.

sources.news_title: Top adviser to Kennedy resigns from Trump administration
sources.text:
Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and central advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has resigned from the Trump administration.
“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement to NBC News. He posted a similar one on X.
Means was an adviser on Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign and a key architect of his MAHA agenda. He joined the White House early last year as a special government employee. He transitioned to a full-time role as senior adviser to the Health and Human Services Department after divesting from his wellness company, Truemed.
A person familiar with Means’ decision to resign said Means had been growing increasingly frustrated as he realized how little he could get done in Washington to advance his MAHA goals.
The final straw, the source said, was the lack of progress on rolling out a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods — one of Means’ biggest priorities. The administration teased a definition in August but has yet to release it.
The source also mentioned Trump’s executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. (glyphosate is the key ingredient in Roundup), as well as some actions at the Environmental Protection Agency that have clashed with Kennedy’s agenda.
Trump’s EPA has, for example, weakened mercury emissions standards and rolled back drinking water limits for certain PFAS chemicals — actions the MAHA movement has largely opposed.
“We are grateful for Calley Means’ time in the Trump Administration. He has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement,” White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement.
Frustrations over a lack of progress on MAHA goals have reverberated throughout the movement. Earlier this month, some supporters — including former members of Kennedy’s presidential campaign — accused the Trump administration of breaking nearly every promise made to them on food, agriculture and environmental health.
With less than two weeks left until the midterm elections, some dissatisfied MAHA supporters have threatened to abstain from voting. Some Democrats are seeking to make inroads with the movement in the final days of campaigning.

On pesticides, a particular setback for the MAHA cause came in June, when the Supreme Court ruled that Bayer, the manufacturer of Roundup, didn’t need to warn consumers about a potential cancer risk associated with its product. The Trump administration had backed Bayer in the case.
President Donald Trump last year nominated Means’ sister, Casey Means, for surgeon general, but she faced scrutiny at her confirmation hearing over her lack of an active medical license and past comments questioning the safety of vaccines and birth control. Trump chose a new nominee, Dr. Nicole Saphier, in April.
Last month, at a talk Means gave at a MAHA summit in Washington, he said he was inspired by the way federal agencies had collaborated to advance the MAHA agenda, but he also acknowledged roadblocks.
“D.C. is a tough place. It’s a toxic place, and there’s a lot of complaints you can make about D.C.,” Means said. “But I am more optimistic today than I’ve ever been about what I feel is my life’s work of evangelizing the chronic disease crisis and empowering Americans who want to be healthy to address the root cause of disease.”
In his statement on Thursday, Means highlighted several policy wins for the MAHA movement during his tenure, including restricting soda purchases through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, fast-tracking research and review of psychedelics, urging food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and overhauling the federal dietary guidelines to recommend less ultraprocessed food and more protein.
“More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history,” he wrote.

sources.news_title: Top MAHA adviser Calley Means resigns from White House days ahead of midterms
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — A top Make America Healthy Again adviser to the Trump administration has resigned, less than two weeks before a midterm election that may serve as a referendum on the MAHA movement.
Calley Means, who joined the administration first as a close adviser to health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and then in the White House, confirmed his departure to STAT. The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed [sic] confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement shared with STAT.
“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started,” he continued.
He didn’t say why he was leaving, but POLITICO reported that it was due to his frustration with delays in releasing a revised definition of ultraprocessed food, which Means was particularly passionate about.
The departure of such a vocal supporter of Kennedy’s agenda puts the MAHA movement on even shakier ground ahead of the elections. With just under two weeks to go, the movement has struggled to find a financial or messaging foothold, with some candidates lagging behind in the polls. Means, from his perch, had pushed back on characterizations that the MAHA movement was faltering, serving as an insider voice witnessing Kennedy at work.
Even prior to joining the administration, Means had been an explosive figure in the MAHA world. He and sister Casey Means gained fame in conservative circles for speaking out against corporate interests in the health care system following the death of their mother, with their 2024 book “Good Energy: The Surprising Connection Between Metabolism and Limitless Health.” Means later was an adviser for Kennedy’s presidential campaign before joining the administration when Kennedy became health secretary.
Casey Means was nominated for surgeon general, but that nomination was pulled after senators expressed concern with her lack of medical experience.
While with the administration, Calley Means was a driving force behind the MAHA agenda as a whole, including a report on chronic disease that included AI-driven errors, and a White House-led effort to expand access to psychedelics. He has been a big supporter of state efforts to limit junk food for SNAP recipients and the remaking of the food pyramid.
Prior to joining the administration, Means was the founder of Truemed, which allows tax-advantaged funds in accounts like FSAs and HSAs to be used to purchase health and wellness products.
This article has been updated with reporting on a potential reason for Means’ departure.

sources.text:
A top ally of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. resigned from the Trump administration on Thursday, reportedly frustrated by White House delays on their food agenda.
Calley Means was a senior adviser to Kennedy and worked in the White House to advance the “Make America Healthy Again” agenda, and he confirmed his exit to the Wall Street Journal but declined to explain it.
“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.,” Means said. “This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”
Sources familiar with the matter told the Journal that Means was deeply frustrated that the White House had delayed some of Kennedy’s most popular ideas. He blamed others in the administration for letting food companies and special interests have too much influence, and one source described him as “disillusioned.”
His departure follows the administration’s decision to hold off on two of Kennedy’s food priorities – an official definition of ultraprocessed foods, meant to eventually lead to labels, and a rule requiring less added sugar and more protein in school meals.
The Journal previously reported that Means had clashed with White House officials in recent months, sometimes raising his voice. Some colleagues found him difficult to work with and unwilling to make practical concessions.
The resignation is a blow to the MAHA movement.
Means helped broker Kennedy’s first call with Trump, which led to their 2024 alliance, and he co-wrote “Good Energy,” a book on diet and the food system that circulated in the Trump campaign, with his sister, Dr. Casey Means. Conservative podcaster Megyn Kelly once called him the “heart of MAHA.”
In the administration, Means helped drive the revised dietary guidelines and inverted food pyramid, the FDA’s push for ingredient transparency, a voluntary phaseout of petroleum-based food dyes and an executive order boosting psychedelics.
It also comes at a bad time for Republicans, who are trying to hold on to MAHA voters ahead of the midterms. Some Kennedy supporters have publicly criticized Trump’s support for pesticides, the slow progress on food policy and the CDC’s continued recommendation of COVID vaccines.
Trump had nominated Casey Means for surgeon general last year, but her nomination collapsed amid senators’ concerns about her vaccine positions.
The White House and HHS didn’t immediately respond to the Journal’s requests for comment.

sources.text:
Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a chief advocate for the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from his position with the Trump administration Thursday.
In a statement, Means did not say why he was leaving. His departure comes as leading voices in the MAHA movement have expressed discontent with what they say is the Trump administration’s lack of progress on a variety of issues, including food security and regulating the weed killer glyphosate.
Means said he “leaves with tremendous respect” for President Donald Trump and Kennedy.
“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick,” Means said. “This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

Means was hired as a White House adviser early in the second Trump administration. He used his perch at the Health and Human Services Department to attack the nation’s leading physician groups, federal agencies and government scientists, claiming they only protect their own interests.
White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration is “grateful” for Means’ time and “he has done a fantastic job for the MAHA movement.” A representative from Health and Human Services did not respond to a request for comment.
Health activist Kelly Ryerson, a leader of American Regeneration who is also known as Glyphosate Girl on social media, said she is “impressed that he completed over two years at HHS fighting the food battle, despite all of the obstacles presented by corporate interests.”
“At the heart of MAHA is a shared belief that the nation’s health must not be sacrificed to corporate profit, and that a preventable slide into chronic disease is a threat to America itself,” she said.
Means is the brother of wellness influencer, author and entrepreneur Dr. Casey Means, who failed to be confirmed as surgeon general earlier this year after doubts were raised over her vaccine stance.

Means, along with his sister, came to prominence within the MAHA movement by arguing that ultraprocessed foods, additives and pesticides could be blamed for many of the chronic health conditions facing Americans.
Means brought those arguments into the Trump administration and frequently clashed with senior White House officials who worried about alienating the powerful food industry.
At the same time, Means’ emphasis on food was a source of frustration for other figures within the MAHA movement who wanted to see Kennedy focus on “medical freedom” issues. For many, that meant rolling back federal recommendations and approvals for vaccines.
Despite Means’ efforts, the administration’s progress on food reforms has been slow going.

sources.text:
Top RFK Jr. Aide’s Yelling White House Meltdown Exposed
Top Trump administration officials and MAHA figures have often clashed over policy.
A leading advocate for Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again campaign got into a yelling match with top White House officials over the definition of processed food, according to a report.
Calley Means, a healthcare entrepreneur who was named a senior adviser to the health secretary last November, met with administration officials to discuss Kennedy’s plans to overhaul the U.S. food system in July.
Means argued in favor of Kennedy’s plans to give processed foods a new label of “ultra-processed” if they contain artificial colors, nonnutritive sweeteners or chemical preservatives, sources told The Wall Street Journal. The White House feared the new definition would cover most foods sold in grocery stores and bolster lawsuits filed against major food manufacturers such as Coca-Cola, WK Kellogg, and Mars, alleging they knowingly made harmful food products.
Means then “raised his voice” during the meeting and expressed his outrage that the White House was pushing back on the plans, insisting the definition change was not up for debate. He claimed that Kennedy’s health department had been working on the ultra-processed foods review for months and had discussed it with scientists.
The fiery meeting was featured in a Journal report detailing how the White House and MAHA supporters have frequently clashed as Kennedy tries to overhaul the U.S. food system.
Means, whom White House officials view as an “overly aggressive” figure who stubbornly tries to implement policies deemed infeasible, is often front and center in these clashes.

He is also the sister of MAHA influencer Casey Means, Donald Trump’s original pick for Surgeon General despite having not having an active medical license.
Earlier this year, the USDA drafted a policy to overhaul the meals schools serve to children that would cost school districts about $2 billion over five years.
Means felt the plans did not go far enough and demanded additional limits on sugar, more protein and 100 percent whole-grain products. Means’ ideas would nearly quadruple the costs of the school meal plans outlined by the government.
During another meeting with government officials about the USDA rules, Means reportedly grew “visibly frustrated” and said that not making the additional, stricter changes would make the Trump administration look like it was “OK with poisoning kids,” the Journal reported.
Following the July meeting on the ultra-processed food definition, the White House decided it needed further review.
However, Kennedy’s team thought they had been given the go-ahead to officially announce the new expanded definition. HHS planned an event to launch the ultra-processed food announcement in August at its headquarters and even decorated the offices with posters depicting “artificial food dye as a monster,” the Journal reported.
However, the ultra-processed food event was pulled, with some White House officials not even aware that the health department planned to unveil it, sources said.
Means and Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, tried again to get the new definition officially released at the end of August, but the White House blocked them, the Journal reported.
“The White House has repeatedly taken on special interests and broken processes to deliver effective and legally durable MAHA policies,” said White House spokesman Kush Desai. “The entire Trump administration continues to work closely with stakeholders and industry leaders to continue overhauling our country’s food and updating nutritional guidance.”
